easy.prompt: What distinguishes supervised from unsupervised learning?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Supervised requires GPUs; unsupervised runs on CPU.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples; unsupervised does not.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Supervised uses neural networks; unsupervised uses decision trees.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Supervised learning fits a function from inputs to labels using (x, y) pairs; unsupervised methods (clustering, density estimation) work from x alone.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hardware doesn't define the learning paradigm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both paradigms use both model families.

easy.prompt: Mean squared error penalizes prediction errors how?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Quadratically — larger errors hurt disproportionately more.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Linearly — every error counts the same per unit.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Not at all — MSE measures variance, not error.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: MSE is the average of squared residuals; doubling an error quadruples its contribution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MSE amplifies, not softens, large errors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes mean absolute error (L1).

easy.prompt: Logistic regression for binary classification outputs…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A probability between 0 and 1 via the sigmoid function.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The raw linear combination of features.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Logistic regression passes wᵀx + b through σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z}) to give P(y = 1 | x).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's linear regression's output before sigmoid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Labels come from thresholding the probability.

easy.prompt: Adding an L2 penalty to a loss function encourages…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: L2 (ridge) adds λ ‖w‖² to the loss, pulling each weight toward zero in proportion to its magnitude.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sparsity comes from L1 (lasso), not L2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Regularization shrinks, it doesn't add features.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate is an optimizer setting, unrelated to the penalty.

easy.prompt: L1 regularization differs from L2 in that L1…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encourages exact zeros, performing implicit feature selection.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: L1 penalty λ∑|wᵢ| has corners on the axes, so the optimum often sits with several weights exactly at zero.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed isn't the distinguishing trait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's L2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's data augmentation or input dropout.

easy.prompt: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) differs from full-batch gradient descent in that SGD…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Estimates the gradient from a single sample or mini-batch each step.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: SGD trades exactness for speed: noisy gradients but many more updates per pass through the data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's Newton's method or quasi-Newton (L-BFGS).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Learning rate is critical for SGD.

easy.prompt: An activation function in a neural network's hidden layer must be non-linear because…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Non-linear functions are faster to compute.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Composing linear layers without non-linearity collapses to a single linear function.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Stacking Wx + b layers without a non-linearity yields another affine map, so depth gives no extra expressive power.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Activations like ReLU are fast, but speed isn't the reason.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Linear functions are trivially differentiable.

easy.prompt: ReLU activation is defined as…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Rectified Linear Unit zeros out negatives and passes positives through unchanged.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Squaring is rarely used as an activation; it's not piecewise-linear.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hyperbolic tangent ranges in (−1, 1) and is smooth everywhere.

easy.prompt: Backpropagation is essentially…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An application of the chain rule for computing gradients of a composed function.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A way to invert matrices quickly.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Backprop traverses the computation graph in reverse, multiplying local Jacobians via the chain rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Clustering is unsupervised; backprop is gradient computation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Backprop computes gradients, not inverses.

easy.prompt: Why split data into training and test sets?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To estimate generalization to unseen data.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Test-set performance is the unbiased estimate of how the model will perform on new data drawn from the same distribution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Class balancing is a separate concern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Holding out data lowers training accuracy if anything.

easy.prompt: The softmax function converts a vector of logits into…

choices.label: B
choices.body: A probability distribution over classes that sums to 1.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: softmax(zᵢ) = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ} normalizes logits into a valid distribution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Softmax outputs are continuous, not binary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Argmax of softmax is one-hot; softmax itself isn't.

easy.prompt: What does cross-validation give you that a single train/test split doesn't?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A lower-variance estimate of generalization performance.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: k-fold CV averages over k splits, reducing the variance of the performance estimate at the cost of k× training.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CV is slower, not faster.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: CV doesn't change model size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: It estimates overfitting; doesn't prevent it.

easy.prompt: Momentum in SGD…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Adds an exponentially weighted average of past gradients to each update.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decreases the learning rate over time.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Momentum smooths the trajectory: v ← βv + ∇L, w ← w − η v. It accelerates along consistent directions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's parallelism, not momentum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a learning-rate schedule, not momentum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Momentum keeps history, doesn't zero gradients.

easy.prompt: Dropout regularizes a network by…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Pruning weights below a threshold permanently.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: At each training step, units are kept with probability p; this prevents co-adaptation and acts like training an ensemble.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: L2 is weight decay; dropout is stochastic.

easy.prompt: Precision and recall measure different aspects of a classifier. Precision is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: TP / (TP + FN) — fraction of actual positives recovered.

choices.label: C
choices.body: TP / (TP + FP) — fraction of predicted positives that are correct.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Precision asks how many of your positive predictions were right.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the false-positive rate (1 − specificity).

easy.prompt: A convolutional layer's key parameter-sharing property means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The same filter is applied at every spatial location.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each output pixel has its own learned weights.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Filters are randomly different at each location.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Sharing filter weights across the input grid gives translation equivariance and dramatically fewer parameters than a dense layer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a dense (fully-connected) layer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each filter has separate per-channel weights; sharing is spatial, not across channels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: There's no sharing in that case.

easy.prompt: An underfitting model exhibits…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Underfit models are too rigid: they miss the signal (high bias) and don't change much with new data (low variance).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's a poorly-fit unstable model — rare for true underfitting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's overfitting.

easy.prompt: An epoch is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: One forward pass on a single example.

choices.label: C
choices.body: One complete pass through the training dataset.

choices.label: D
choices.body: One evaluation on the test set.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: After processing every training example once (in batches), one epoch has elapsed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a single example, not an epoch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Evaluation isn't part of an epoch's definition.

easy.prompt: Cross-entropy loss for a true class y and predicted distribution p is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: −log p(y) — negative log-likelihood of the true class.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Cross-entropy with one-hot targets reduces to −log p(y); minimizing it maximizes the likelihood of the true labels.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's MSE applied to one-hot labels — not standard for classification.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's L1.

easy.prompt: Batch normalization normalizes activations using statistics computed…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Once at initialization and never again.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Per mini-batch during training, with running averages used at inference.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: BN standardizes (x − μ_B) / σ_B on each batch and learns a scale/shift; running estimates of μ, σ are kept for inference.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's layer normalization or instance normalization.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reversed — train-time normalization is the whole point.

medium.prompt: Adam combines two ideas from prior optimizers. Which?

choices.label: D
choices.body: Momentum (first-moment estimate) and per-parameter adaptive learning rates (second-moment estimate).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Adam tracks m_t (moving average of gradients) and v_t (moving average of squared gradients), correcting bias and adapting the step per parameter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Neither idea is part of Adam.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adam updates all parameters per step.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Adam doesn't use exact Hessian information.

medium.prompt: Why does logistic regression use the log-loss (cross-entropy) rather than MSE?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Log-loss is convex in the parameters and is the negative log-likelihood under the model.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Under the Bernoulli model, the MLE objective is precisely log-loss; MSE on sigmoid outputs is non-convex and has vanishing gradients far from 0.5.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Log-loss is gradient-based like any loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Speed isn't the reason; convexity and likelihood are.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MSE can be defined, but loses the MLE interpretation and convexity.

medium.prompt: Early stopping regularizes by…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Halting training when validation loss stops improving, implicitly constraining model capacity.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Early stopping effectively limits how far parameters can move from initialization, similar in spirit to L2 in some regimes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a separate technique.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stopping is about when to halt, not step size.

medium.prompt: Vanishing gradients in deep networks arise primarily when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The learning rate is too large.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Gradients are explicitly set to zero.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Activations or weights repeatedly compress gradient magnitudes through many layers.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Sigmoids saturate, and chained Jacobians with norms < 1 shrink the signal exponentially with depth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Large LR causes explosion, not vanishing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's gradient clipping with threshold 0, not the natural cause.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Batch size affects variance, not systematic vanishing.

medium.prompt: If a 5×5 input is convolved with a 3×3 kernel using stride 1 and no padding, the output has size…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Output size = (input − kernel) / stride + 1 = (5 − 3)/1 + 1 = 3.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Would require 'same' padding.

medium.prompt: Adding more training data primarily reduces…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Bias, with limited effect on variance.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Variance, with limited effect on bias.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: More data tightens the estimator's distribution (less variance) but doesn't change the model's expressivity (bias).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Variance shrinks much faster with data than bias does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Bias is mostly about model capacity, not data quantity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Data quantity matters substantially.

medium.prompt: Xavier (Glorot) initialization picks weight variances to…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Randomize signs only, leaving magnitude fixed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Keep the variance of activations and gradients roughly constant across layers.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Variance ∝ 1/(fan-in + fan-out) keeps the forward signal and backward gradient at similar scale.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Glorot is a distribution, not a constant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: All-zero init breaks symmetry and prevents learning.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's sign initialization, not Xavier.

medium.prompt: An ROC curve plots…

choices.label: A
choices.body: True positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: ROC sweeps the decision threshold, plotting TPR vs FPR; AUC measures area under it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a training curve.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Not a standard plot.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's a PR curve, not ROC.

medium.prompt: Learning-rate warmup is most useful when…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Training large models with adaptive optimizers like Adam, to avoid destabilizing early steps.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Warmup linearly ramps the LR from 0 to its target, letting Adam's running statistics stabilize before large updates.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Label noise is a different problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Warmup isn't tied to batch size of 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Warmup is more about stable large-scale training.

medium.prompt: The bias-variance decomposition for squared loss writes the expected error as…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: E[(ŷ − y)²] = (bias)² + var + σ² when targets have inherent noise σ².

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Only bias is squared in the decomposition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Missing the irreducible noise term.

medium.prompt: Pooling layers (max or average) primarily provide…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Spatial downsampling and a small amount of translation invariance.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Pooling shrinks the spatial dimensions and gives a coarse invariance to small shifts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pooling has no parameters.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Max-pool is non-linear but isn't ReLU.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Pooling isn't stochastic in the same sense.

medium.prompt: Why do plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies?

choices.label: D
choices.body: Gradients vanish or explode as they're propagated through many time steps.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Repeated multiplication by the recurrent Jacobian over many steps shrinks or blows up gradients exponentially.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Parameter sharing across time is exactly what RNNs do.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: They typically use tanh or ReLU.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: RNNs handle variable-length sequences.

medium.prompt: LSTM and GRU mitigate vanishing gradients by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Introducing gated additive paths so information can flow over many steps without repeated multiplication.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The cell state in an LSTM accumulates additively; the gates control writes and reads, preserving gradient magnitude.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: More layers can worsen the problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Gates use sigmoid, but that alone doesn't fix vanishing.

medium.prompt: Double descent describes the phenomenon where…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Training error always doubles before halving.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The learning rate must be set in two phases.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Adding regularization doubles the test error.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Test error decreases, rises, then decreases again as model capacity grows past the interpolation threshold.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Over-parameterized models can generalize well past the classical U-shape, giving a second descent in test error.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a schedule, not double descent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Regularization usually lowers it.

medium.prompt: Why is cross-entropy preferred over MSE for classification?

choices.label: A
choices.body: MSE only works for regression problems with integer targets.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It penalizes confident wrong predictions much more strongly, giving stronger gradients near the wrong class.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Cross-entropy's gradient with respect to logits is (p − y), which doesn't vanish for confident wrong predictions the way MSE-on-sigmoid does.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: MSE works on any real targets.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Compute is comparable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Calibration isn't automatic.

medium.prompt: Gradient clipping is most commonly used to address…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Exploding gradients, especially in RNN training.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Clipping ‖∇‖ to a max norm prevents single huge updates from destabilizing the optimizer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Clipping doesn't help when gradients are too small.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Step-size schedules help convergence; clipping handles spikes.

medium.prompt: Train-test data leakage means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The training set is too large.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Information from the test set has influenced model training or selection.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Common leaks: tuning hyperparameters on the test set, computing normalization stats over all data, or duplicate samples across splits.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's an unlabeled-test problem, not leakage.

medium.prompt: Weight decay in SGD is equivalent to which regularizer (in the simplest sense)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Adding λw to the gradient is the derivative of (λ/2) ‖w‖², so SGD with weight decay implements L2.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Augmentation transforms inputs; weight decay penalizes weights.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Dropout is stochastic; weight decay is deterministic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: L1's gradient is sign(w), not w.

medium.prompt: Why does data augmentation often improve generalization?

choices.label: B
choices.body: It expands the effective training distribution, exposing the model to nuisance variations.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It reduces the number of parameters.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Augmentations encode invariances (rotation, crop, color jitter) so the model learns features robust to them.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Augmentation typically slows training.

medium.prompt: The softmax+cross-entropy gradient with respect to logits z is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: p − y, where p is the softmax output and y is one-hot.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: This clean form is one reason softmax + cross-entropy is the canonical pairing for classification.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's σ's derivative for a single sigmoid output.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Not a valid gradient form.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That would be a squared loss, not its gradient.

hard.prompt: Adam's bias correction (m̂_t = m_t / (1 − β₁^t)) addresses…

choices.label: D
choices.body: The initial under-estimate of the moving averages caused by zero initialization.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Because m_0 = 0, m_t is biased toward zero for small t; dividing by 1 − β₁^t un-biases the estimate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Optimizer doesn't address imbalance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Numerical stability is handled by the ε term.

hard.prompt: Why can over-parameterized neural networks generalize well despite fitting the training data exactly?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The training data is always linearly separable.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Modern GPUs round gradients in a regularizing way.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Implicit bias of SGD selects low-norm or smooth interpolating solutions among many possible ones.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Dropout is the only thing that makes it work.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Among interpolating models, SGD tends to find solutions in flat / low-norm regions that generalize; this is an active research area.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Numerical noise isn't the explanation.

hard.prompt: A 1×1 convolution is best understood as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A per-pixel linear combination across channels — essentially a channel-wise MLP applied independently at each spatial location.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: 1×1 convs mix channels without changing spatial layout; used heavily in bottlenecks (Inception, ResNets).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Normalization standardizes statistics, not linear mix.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Pooling doesn't have learnable weights per channel.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only if weights are exactly identity; in general it's learned.

hard.prompt: Self-attention's computational cost scales with sequence length n as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: O(n²) in time and memory for the attention matrix.

choices.label: B
choices.body: O(d²) where d is the embedding dim, independent of n.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Each token attends to every other, giving an n × n attention matrix; reducing this is an active research area (linear attention, sparse attention).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Per-token projections are O(d²) but attention itself is n-dependent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Not a standard cost class for attention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Linear attention variants exist but plain self-attention is quadratic.

hard.prompt: Layer normalization vs batch normalization: layer norm computes statistics over…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The features of a single example, independent of the batch.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Time and channel dimensions of the batch jointly.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Layer norm is per-example, which makes it suitable for variable-length sequences and small batches.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the opposite of what layer norm does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That mixes examples — would be batch-like.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Norms operate on activations, not labels.

hard.prompt: The cross-entropy decomposes as H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p ‖ q). For one-hot p, this becomes…

choices.label: A
choices.body: KL(p ‖ q) — H(p) is zero because p is deterministic.

choices.label: D
choices.body: −log q only when q is one-hot too.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: A deterministic distribution has zero entropy, so minimizing cross-entropy reduces to minimizing KL divergence to the empirical label.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: H(p) = 0 for one-hot p.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Only if q = p exactly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: −log q is the cross-entropy for any q; one-hot q would be 0 or ∞.

hard.prompt: The convergence rate of plain gradient descent on a smooth convex function is…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: For L-smooth convex objectives, after t steps f(x_t) − f* ≤ O(1/t); strongly convex gives geometric (e^{−t}-style) convergence.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's strongly convex, not just smooth convex.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's subgradient method on non-smooth convex functions.

hard.prompt: Mixed-precision training stores most computations in lower precision (e.g., FP16) but keeps a master copy in FP32. Why?

choices.label: C
choices.body: To preserve numerical stability of small updates that would underflow in FP16.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Tiny gradient updates can be smaller than the FP16 smallest representable step; an FP32 master copy accumulates them without loss.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TPU/GPU compatibility differs by hardware; not the reason.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Labels are typically integers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mixed-precision is for training, not deployment compression.

hard.prompt: Why does the no-free-lunch theorem matter in practice?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It means more data is always worse than less.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It says deep learning always wins.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No learning algorithm is universally best; performance depends on the data distribution's structure.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Averaged over all possible problems, every algorithm performs equally; practical wins come from matching inductive bias to the data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CV is fine; NFL is about algorithm universality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Opposite — no method wins everywhere.

hard.prompt: Residual connections (skip connections) help training primarily by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Doubling the number of features per layer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Providing identity gradient paths that mitigate optimization difficulty in deep networks.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Forcing each layer to learn the identity.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Allowing y = x + F(x) means at worst a layer can pass the signal through; gradients flow unimpeded through the skip path.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The opposite — they make the identity easy when useful, not required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Skip connections aren't a regularizer in this sense.

hard.prompt: SGD with replacement and SGD without replacement (random reshuffling) differ in that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both produce identical iterates given the same seed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Random reshuffling typically converges faster in practice; with replacement is easier to analyze theoretically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Random reshuffling requires sorting the data.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random reshuffling is unbiased; with replacement is biased.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Theory often assumes replacement (i.i.d.) for clean bounds; practice prefers reshuffling per epoch for empirical speedup.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sampling rule differs, so iterates differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No sorting — just permutation.

hard.prompt: Focal loss modifies cross-entropy by…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Computing loss only on the top-k predictions.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replacing softmax with sigmoid for multi-class.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Down-weighting easy examples via a (1 − p_t)^γ factor, focusing learning on hard ones.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Focal loss = −(1 − p_t)^γ log p_t; high-confidence correct predictions contribute little, useful for heavily imbalanced detection tasks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Top-k isn't part of focal loss.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a separate change.

hard.prompt: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) seeks parameters that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Are the global minimum of the loss exactly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Minimize the worst-case loss in a neighborhood around w, encouraging flat minima.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Lie on a specific sphere of the parameter space.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: SAM updates use ∇L at w + ε, where ε is the adversarial perturbation; this biases toward flat regions correlated with generalization.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Opposite of flat minima.

hard.prompt: In a Transformer, positional encodings are necessary because…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Self-attention is order-invariant; without positional information, token order is lost.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Permuting input tokens produces a permuted output unless positional encodings break the symmetry.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Optimizer doesn't see positions.

hard.prompt: Why does using a too-large learning rate often cause loss to diverge in deep networks?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each step overshoots local curvature, amplifying parameter updates and gradient magnitudes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The optimizer runs out of memory.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: With LR > 2/L (L = local Lipschitz constant), GD on a quadratic diverges; in deep nets the effective L can be very large.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: LR doesn't affect memory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Floating-point weights stay continuous.

hard.prompt: MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on weights is equivalent to MLE with…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Log of a Gaussian prior contributes −(λ/2) ‖w‖² to the log-posterior, identical to L2 weight decay.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: L1 corresponds to a Laplace prior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropout has a Bayesian interpretation but a different one.

hard.prompt: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a large teacher to a small student by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pruning the teacher to fit the student's size.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Training the student to match the teacher's soft probability outputs (often with a temperature).

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Soft targets carry richer information than hard labels (dark knowledge); temperature smooths the distribution.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Architectures usually differ; you can't copy directly.

hard.prompt: Depthwise separable convolutions reduce computation by…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Splitting standard convolution into per-channel spatial filtering followed by 1×1 channel mixing.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: If standard cost is k² · C_in · C_out, separable is k² · C_in + C_in · C_out — a major saving when C_out is large.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Spatial filtering is preserved per channel.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Opposite direction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Weights are already shared across batches.

hard.prompt: Label smoothing replaces one-hot targets with…

choices.label: B
choices.body: (1 − α) on the true class and α/(K − 1) on each other class.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Label smoothing tempers overconfidence and often improves calibration with marginal accuracy cost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would corrupt training.

hard.prompt: Why does ensembling typically improve test accuracy over any single model in the ensemble?

choices.label: D
choices.body: Averaging predictions cancels uncorrelated errors, reducing variance of the predictor.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: If errors of base models are partially independent, the averaged predictor has lower variance and often lower expected error.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Bias reduces only if base models systematically err in different directions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Ensembles are larger, not smaller.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each model still needs training data.
